Various critical items are not widely available outside China: (1) quartz crucibles, diamond wire, and other manufacturing equipment most suitable for PV ingot and wafer production; (2) screen-printable metallization pastes for cell production; and (3) PV- specialized glass, junction boxes, electrical diodes within junction boxes, and cell stringing, tabbing, and bussing ribbons for module assembly. Manufacturing equipment for ingots, wafers, cells, and modules is not widely available from U.S. suppliers and is generally lowest cost from Chinese suppliers. While the United States is developing a local supply chain, it is challenging to achieve economies of scale. 2.2 Global Context More than 98% of global PV module manufacturing capacity was c-Si in 2024 (Figure 5). The c- Si supply chain has primarily scaled in Asia since 2010, mostly in China. ASEAN also hosts significant manufacturing centers owing to its proximity to China and its low labor costs as well as U.S. trade policies that hinder direct imports from China. Figure 5. Global PV annual manufacturing capacities in 2024. Data source: “Solar Manufacturing Assets” Database, Accessed December 2024 (BNEF 2025b) Much of the c-Si manufacturing capacity in Asia was underutilized in 2024, as large investments in manufacturing capacity made during 2019–2023 led to oversupply by the second half of 2023. Over 1,000 GW of global PV manufacturing capacity existed at the end of 2024, but only 580 dc GW of PV was installed (BNEF 2025b). Longer term, the dc continuation of global oversupply conditions depends on Chinese industrial policies and the balance sheets of firms operating there. U.S. policies have sought to support domestic PV manufacturing, including using tariffs and AD/CVD duties, which raise the administrative burden and prices for imports. Since the original AD/CVD cases against China in 2011, a large difference between U.S. module prices and prices elsewhere has persisted. In 2024, U.S. module prices were $250–$350/kW compared with $80– dc $120/kW in the rest of the world (Feldman, Zuboy, Dummit, Heine, Narayanaswami, et al. dc 2025). While global PV manufacturers enjoy higher profits in the U.S. market, they must manage supply chain considerations and logistics, which has driven a change in the source of U.S. imports over the past 15 years. Considerations include the following: • UFLPA inspection: Manufacturers of detained products must provide rigorous documentation for materials as far upstream as mg-Si—and sometimes even to the originally mined silica.
